spoken: At five twenty in the morning on the 4th of November 1956, Prime Minister Im-reh Nodge spoke on the radio for 35 seconds.
Soviet troops were attacking Budapest. Our troops are in combat, he said. The Government is at its post.
Within a week, the armed resistance was crushed. Hungary's workers held out without weapons until mid-December.
This is the story of those weeks.
On the 3rd of November, Hungary's government was negotiating the withdrawal of Soviet troops.
But on the 31st of October, as their own notes show, the Soviet leaders had secretly decided to crush the revolution.
Near midnight, Soviet security police arrested the Hungarian negotiators, among them Defence Minister Pahl Mah-lay-ter.
At four fifteen in the morning on the 4th of November, Soviet forces attacked Budapest and towns across Hungary.
By the count of the military historian Mik-lohsh Hor-vaht, about 60,000 soldiers from parts of 17 divisions took part.
The Hungarian army, ordered by its generals not to resist, was disarmed almost everywhere.
Many Soviet soldiers were conscripts from far away. Some, witnesses told the UN, believed they were in Egypt, at Suez.
At five oh five, another station had announced a new government under Yah-nosh Kah-dahr.
It was said to be in Sol-nok, but the 1956 Institute places it in Oozh-horod, in Soviet Ukraine.
On paper, Kah-dahr was still one of Nodge's ministers, but on the 1st of November he had vanished and been flown to Moscow.
His government called the uprising a counter-revolution, and said it had asked the Soviet army for help.
At five twenty, Im-reh Nodge spoke on Free Radio Ko-shoot. At about six, he left Parliament for the Yugoslav embassy.
At seven fifty-seven, the Writers' Union called on the world's writers and scholars to help Hungary.
At eight oh seven, Free Radio Ko-shoot fell silent.
One minister stayed at his post in Parliament as the Soviet soldiers came. He was Isht-vahn Bee-boh.
He wrote that Hungarians should not recognise the occupiers or their puppet government as lawful.
He called for every means of passive resistance, but asked them to spare Budapest's water and public services.
Young fighters and workers fought on, hoping to hold out until the world acted.
In Budapest, the Corvin passage fell on the morning of the 6th of November, after an artillery attack.
The working districts held out longest. They were Ooy-pest in the north, and Cheh-pell in the south.
At Cheh-pell, workers and the local army unit fought together.
On the 9th of November, Soviet artillery shelled the town centre. Fifty-four people died there that day, whole families among them.
That evening, Cheh-pell's defence was broken.
In the steel town of Doona-pen-teleh, then named Stah-leen-vah-rosh, workers and soldiers stood together too.
Its radio called for help in Hungarian and German. On the 7th of November, the town was bombed and shelled, and fell.
Near Paych, several hundred men held out in the Meh-chek hills until the 19th of November, then walked to Yugoslavia.
By the 11th of November, the organised armed resistance was broken.
How many died? Early in 1957, the Statistical Office counted 2,502 known deaths in the whole uprising.
Recent research puts the total at about 2,700. Most sources give 2,500 to 3,000 Hungarian dead.
The Soviet army counted 720 of its own soldiers dead.
They were students and workers, soldiers and passers-by, young and old, and Soviet conscripts far from home.
In the Yugoslav embassy, Nodge was joined by ministers, writers and their families, with seventeen children.
Outside stood Soviet tanks. Kah-dahr's government, sworn in on the 7th of November, wanted them out.
Nodge had not resigned, and while he was free, Kah-dahr's claim to govern was in doubt.
Belgrade asked for a written guarantee that the group could go home freely. Kah-dahr proposed Romania instead, and Nodge refused.
On the 21st of November, Kah-dahr promised in writing that they would face no sanctions for their past activities.
The next evening, a bus came to take them home, and Soviet soldiers insisted on boarding it.
At the Soviet command, the two Yugoslav diplomats on board were ordered off, and the bus drove away under armoured escort.
The group was flown to Romania. Kah-dahr's government said they had asked to go.
The UN committee found that they were taken by force, without even being told where.
In April 1957, Nodge was arrested in Romania and brought back to Hungary for a secret trial.
The guns fell quiet, but the factories stood still. Nowhere did work resume.
The workers' councils, elected in the factories since October, now led the resistance.
On the 14th of November, they formed the Central Workers' Council of Greater Budapest, chaired by Shahn-dor Rahts, aged 23.
They demanded the withdrawal of Soviet troops, free elections and Nodge's return.
Kah-dahr promised a great deal. But when they asked for it in writing, he said his word should be enough.
On the 21st of November, Soviet tanks blocked a national meeting of the councils, and Budapest struck for forty-eight hours.
On the 4th of December, several thousand women walked in silence to Heroes' Square with flowers.
Soviet soldiers were waiting, but India's ambassador came too, and the women laid their flowers.
On the 8th of December in Shahl-goh-tar-yahn, a mining town, some 4,000 people demanded the release of two arrested council leaders.
Security forces, police and Soviet soldiers fired into the crowd. How the shooting began is still disputed.
Forty-six of the dead are known by name, and estimates run higher.
On the 9th of December, the government banned the Central Workers' Council.
On the 11th of December, Kah-dahr invited Rahts and the council's secretary, Shahn-dor Bah-lee, to Parliament, where they were arrested.
The strike of the 11th and 12th of December was the last. By mid-December, out of sheer need, work resumed.
Why did no help come? At the UN, the Soviet Union vetoed action in the Security Council.
On the 4th of November, the General Assembly called on it to withdraw, by 50 votes to 8. Moscow and Kah-dahr ignored it.
In the same days, Israel, Britain and France attacked Egypt over the Suez Canal, and the United States opposed them.
The United States condemned the Soviet attack, but would not risk a world war over Hungary.
On the 27th of October, Secretary of State Dulles had said, we do not look upon these nations as potential military allies.
Radio Free Europe, broadcasting from Munich with American money, had encouraged the fighters.
Its own review found no direct promise of military help, with one exception.
On the 4th of November, it quoted a London paper suggesting that American help might come if Hungarians held out.
Many listeners heard a promise. In a survey of a thousand refugees in Austria, 96 percent had trusted in some American help.
The fighters held out for a week, the workers for five. By mid-December, the revolution had been crushed.
By then, refugees were crossing the border, some 200,000 in all, and the reprisals had begun.
For over thirty years, the regime called 1956 a counter-revolution. What it left behind is the next part of the story.
